original_value: Many successful methods have been proposed for learning low dimensional representations on large-scale networks, while almost all existing methods are designed in inseparable processes, learning embeddings for entire networks even when only a small proportion of nodes are of interest. This leads to great inconvenience, especially on super-large or dynamic networks, where these methods become almost impossible to implement. In this paper, we formalize the problem of separated matrix factorization, based on which we elaborate a novel objective function that preserves both local and global information. We further propose SepNE, a simple and flexible network embedding algorithm which independently learns representations for different subsets of nodes in separated processes. By implementing separability, our algorithm reduces the redundant efforts to embed irrelevant nodes, yielding scalability to super-large networks, automatic implementation in distributed learning and further adaptations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on several real-world networks with different scales and subjects. With comparable accuracy, our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in running times on large networks.

result.paraphrase: Many successful methods have been proposed for learning low-dimensional representations on large-scale networks, yet nearly all existing approaches use inseparable procedures that learn embeddings for whole networks even when only a small fraction of nodes is of interest. This creates considerable inconvenience, particularly for super-large or dynamic networks, where such methods become almost impractical to deploy. In this paper, we formalize the problem of separated matrix factorization and, on that basis, develop a new objective function that preserves both local and global information. We also present SepNE, a simple and flexible network embedding algorithm that independently learns representations for different subsets of nodes through separated processes. By introducing separability, our method avoids redundant effort on embedding irrelevant nodes, enabling scalability to super-large networks, automatic implementation in distributed learning, and further extensions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on several real-world networks of varying scales and domains. With comparable accuracy, our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in running time on large networks.
